```{=html}
<h2 id='skyRadiance'>Inspect the linear light field of a natural sky</h2><span id='topic+skyRadiance'></span>

<h3>Description</h3>

<p>Samples a natural sketch before display compression or masking by local
terrain. One integrated flux unit is a magnitude-zero V-band source.
</p>


<h3>Usage</h3>

<pre><code class='language-R'>skyRadiance(sky, xrange = c(0, 360), yrange = c(0, 90), size = c(720, 180))
</code></pre>


<h3>Arguments</h3>

<table role = "presentation">
<tr><td><code id="skyRadiance_+3A_sky">sky</code></td>
<td>
<p>A natural sketch from <code>sketchSky</code>.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="skyRadiance_+3A_xrange">xrange</code></td>
<td>
<p>Increasing true azimuth limits in degrees. A sector may cross
north, for example c(340,380).</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="skyRadiance_+3A_yrange">yrange</code></td>
<td>
<p>Increasing altitude limits within -90 to 90 degrees.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="skyRadiance_+3A_size">size</code></td>
<td>
<p>Positive integer column and row counts, up to 1600 by 1000.</p>
</td></tr>
</table>


<h3>Details</h3>

<p>Direct light includes stars, residual cluster light, planetary discs
and the illuminated lunar disc. The Milky Way uses the accepted tracing and
a provisional Carina surface-brightness calibration. Stars remain unresolved
as the view is enlarged. See <code>sketchSky</code> for sources, assumptions
and interpretation.
</p>


<h3>Value</h3>

<p>A list containing azimuth and altitude pixel centres, total radiance,
direct light (stars, residual cluster light, planets and lunar disc), and
Milky Way radiance. Matrices are in magnitude-zero flux units per square
degree, ordered from high to low altitude and increasing azimuth. Multiply
by area (square degrees per pixel by row) and sum to obtain flux. The
difference between total and the two source matrices is the atmospheric
background. The Sun contributes to the background; its disc is a plot overlay.
</p>


<h3>Observational validation</h3>

<p>Across 56 recorded dates, heliacal rising fell within seven days of 22 of 23 first morning sightings. The median prediction was two days early. Acronycal setting fell within seven days of 21 of 33 last evening sightings. The median prediction was five days late. A week is a practical search window. Larger discrepancies occur, especially at dusk. These results apply to the two tested events. <a href="heliacal-rising.html#v01-observations">V01 observed dates and scientific checks</a>.
</p>


<h3>Scientific checks</h3>


<ul>
<li><p> First-morning dates fell within seven days of 22 of 23 sightings and last-evening dates within seven days of 21 of 33. The respective median predictions were two days early and five days late. <a href="heliacal-rising.html#v01-observations">V01 study</a>.
</p>
</li>
<li><p> The Milky Way lookup recovered all 4,323,600 stored classes and agreed across the longitude seam. Independent tracing of the outline remains open. <a href="sky-rendering.html#mw-grid-check">V02 study</a>.
</p>
</li>
<li><p> Twilight brightness had a mean absolute residual of 0.481 magnitudes against 22 held-out measurements. This benchmark covers twilight only. <a href="sky-rendering.html#twilight-check">V03 study</a>.
</p>
</li>
<li><p> Across six independent diffuse-light fields the residuals had both signs. The Carina normalisation alone could not account for the spatial differences. <a href="v04-diffuse-photometry.html">V04 study</a>.
</p>
</li>
<li><p> With extinction of 0.2 magnitudes per airmass, transmission was 0.149 at 5 degrees and 0.832 at the zenith under the adopted law. <a href="sky-rendering.html#extinction-check">V05 study</a>.
</p>
</li></ul>


```
